full_judgment:
2. Basharat Ali respondent since deceased and substituted by his heirs transferred the suit land to Abdul Quddus appellant by a registered kabala dated 20-10-1950. By a contemporaneous oral agreement entered into between the same parties the appellant Abdul Quddus agreed to re-convey the land on repayment of the consideration within the month of Chaitra in any year. The appellant Abdul Quddus returned the consideration to the respondent Basharat Ali in the first part of Chaitra, 1371 B.S. corresponding to the second part of March, 1965. On the appellant's failure to execute and register the kabala on demand, the respondent Basharat Ali as plaintiff instituted the suit which was decreed by the trial court and affirmed by the Court of First Appeal as stated above. 

 4. The next question that I proceed to examine is whether the contract was bad for uncertainty. Section 29 of the Contract Act provides that agreements, the meaning of which is not certain, or capable of being made certain, are void. None of the illustrations (a) to (f) to that section suggests that if the time for performance of contract is not fixed the contract would be void for uncertainty. On the other hand section 46 of the Contract Act provides that where, by the contract, a promissory is to perform his promise without application by the promise, and no time for performance is specified, the engagement must be performed within a reasonable time. In other words section 46 is clear to show that mere non-specification of time of performance of contract will not make the contract void and that the contract has to be performed within a reasonable time. The learned Advocate could not also place any decision in support of his contention that if no time is specified for performance of a contract the contract will be void for uncertainty. It may be added that in the instant case it is evident that the plaintiff was to perform his promise without application by the defendant promise. The learned Advocate has next submitted that such a contract is required to be performed within a reasonable time as provided in section 46 of the Contract Act. He submits that in the instant case the contract was made on 20-10-1950 and the plaintiff returned the consideration money in March, 1965 i.e. about 14 years after the contract. It cannot be said to be performance of the promise within a reasonable time and as such the Courts below have erred in law in giving a decree for the specific performance of the contract. The explanation to section 46 of the Contract Act provides that the question "what is a reasonable time" is, in each particular case, a question of fact. In the case of Gladstone Wyllie & Co. Ltd. V. A.B.M. Shayesta Khan and another decided by a Division Bench of this Court and reported in 28 D.L.R. 344 the Court held that what is reasonable time is undoubtedly dependent upon the facts and circumstances of each case. In the reported case the court was dealing with the meaning of reasonable time within the meaning of section 6(2) of the Contract Act. That section has not defined or explained what a reasonable time is but even then Court held that what was reasonable time was dependent upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The explanation to section 46 of the Contract Act, however, clearly says that "what is reasonable time" is, in each particular case, a question of fact. In the case before me it has been proved that the plaintiff paid the money after about 14 years and the evidence has also showed that the money was accepted by the defendant. The Conduct of the Parties clearly proves that the parties themselves considered the time within which the consideration was returned to be a reasonable time and this Court has no reason to take a view which would be inconsistent with the conduct of the parties. In the instant case, therefore, it must be held that the promise was performed within a reasonable time. In view of my discussions above I find to reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court affirming those of the trial Court.
